edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SCIENCE & TECH + SPORT
edition.deck: Iran’s latest strike on Bahrain, a disputed Ukraine peace proposal and fresh political and legal tests in Denmark lead tonight’s coverage.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments and fresh reporting. Returning stories are included only where the gather adds a meaningful update; allegations and proposals remain clearly attributed.

content.headline: Iran says it targeted a US air-defence site in Bahrain with six drones
content.shortHeadline: Iran says it targeted a US air-defence site in Bahrain
content.standfirst: Bahrain says its defences intercepted the drones, in Iran’s second attack on the country in three days. The strikes come amid a standoff over the Strait of Hormuz, where shipping remains restricted.

image.caption: Iran and the US are vying for control of the Strait of Hormuz.

sources.originalTitle: Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack

segments.body: Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said it sent six drones towards a US air-defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base on Sunday. Bahrain’s military said its air defences intercepted and destroyed the attack before it could achieve its aims. There were no reported injuries or damage in this account.

segments.title: A wider standoff
segments.body: The attack follows an earlier Iranian drone strike on Bahrain on Friday. The US and Iran remain at odds over the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and gas shipments. Iran says it should control the strait; the US says it is protecting tankers serving Gulf Arab states.

content.headline: Zelensky says US envoys raised trading Donbas withdrawal for Nato membership
content.shortHeadline: Zelensky says US raised Donbas withdrawal for Nato membership
content.standfirst: Ukraine’s president says US negotiators asked whether Kyiv would leave the Donbas in exchange for Nato membership. Washington has not confirmed the proposal, and Zelensky says any concrete offer would need security guarantees and a public vote.

image.caption: Volodymyr Zelensky said the US had proposed a new peace plan.

sources.originalTitle: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
Zelensky reveals glimpse at Ukraine’s Nato membership – but it comes with a catch

segments.body: Volodymyr Zelensky says US envoys raised the possibility of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the Donbas in return for Nato membership. A US official told the BBC that many ideas are being discussed and any final agreement would need both sides’ approval. No specific offer has been confirmed.

segments.title: Unresolved terms
segments.body: Zelensky says he would put a concrete proposal to a referendum if it included security guarantees, funding to rebuild Ukraine and no limits on its armed forces. The reports also describe continuing disagreement over territory and the conditions for a peace deal; neither a settlement nor Ukraine’s membership of Nato has been agreed.

perspectives.body: The i Paper reports that recent US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi ended without a major breakthrough, though the sides agreed to a prisoner exchange involving more than 1,000 people, according to Zelensky.

content.headline: Prague protest draws hundreds of thousands over plans to change public media
content.shortHeadline: Hundreds of thousands protest Czech public media plan
content.standfirst: Organisers put the crowd at about 350,000, opposing plans to replace licence fees with state funding. They fear the change could give ministers more leverage over public broadcasters; the government says claims of interference are unfounded.

sources.originalTitle: Protest in Prague over media freedom expected to be one of biggest in Czechia’s history

segments.body: An estimated 350,000 people joined a protest in Prague on Sunday against the government’s plan to end licence fees and fund public television and radio from the state budget. The estimate is from the organisers, Million Moments for Democracy. The proposed changes would cut the broadcasters’ budgets by about 15%.

segments.title: A dispute over independence
segments.body: Protesters say state funding could give ministers more influence over newsrooms, and public media staff have also staged a strike. Prime Minister Andrej Babiš rejects the criticism, calling claims that the plan threatens media freedom unfounded and saying the government will not interfere in editorial work.

content.headline: Megaspeed opens inquiry amid scrutiny of Nvidia chip exports to China
content.shortHeadline: Megaspeed opens inquiry into Nvidia chip-export allegations
content.standfirst: The Singapore-based data-centre company says it has begun an internal investigation after allegations that chips may have reached Chinese firms through its operations. It rejects claims it says lack verifiable evidence.

sources.originalTitle: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
Nvidia scandal: US treasury chief blames Lutnick’s commerce department over alleged lack of action

segments.body: Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia, says it has retained external lawyers to investigate its business and supply chain. The company is suspected of providing Chinese firms with access to restricted chips through data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand; those claims have not been established.

segments.title: Questions over oversight
segments.body: The controversy has prompted scrutiny of US export controls and the Commerce Department’s role. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said agencies had favoured placing Megaspeed on a trade blacklist for months, while the department had yet to do so. Congressional hearings and requests for records are also expected.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that lawmakers from both parties are pressing for investigations and hearings, with questions also being raised about what senior administration officials knew and when.

content.headline: Russian police chief accused of leading kidnappings to send men to Ukraine
content.shortHeadline: Russian police chief accused of abducting men for Ukraine war
content.standfirst: A regional police chief in Russia is in custody on suspicion of leading a group that forced socially vulnerable men to sign military contracts. Investigators allege the group sought payments intended for recruits or their families.

image.caption: Yuriy Shibayev at a court hearing; he denies the allegations.

source.credit: Foto: / Ivanovo regional court press service / VKontakte

sources.originalTitle: Politichef sigtes for at stå bag kidnapning af russiske alkoholikere til Putins krig

segments.body: Yuriy Shibayev, until recently head of police in the Komsomolsky district of Ivanovo, is suspected of leading a group that abducted local men and forced them to sign contracts to fight in Ukraine, according to Russian media cited by TV 2. Shibayev denies the allegations and is being held in custody until 2 January 2027.

segments.title: A wider pattern alleged
segments.body: Investigators say the group tried to obtain payments from the defence ministry intended for the recruits or their relatives. The case reportedly involves 15 people and at least seven victims. TV 2 says it could not establish whether one man described by a partner as having been taken by force is among them; similar allegations have been reported in other Russian regions.

content.headline: Ebola outbreak in DR Congo remains uncontrolled, Africa CDC chief warns
content.shortHeadline: Ebola outbreak in DR Congo remains uncontrolled
content.standfirst: More than 11,200 people have been infected and 5,500 have died since the outbreak began in May, according to Africa CDC. A Congolese doctor who survived the disease is trying to counter fear and mistrust that can delay treatment.

sources.originalTitle: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
Africa CDC: Ebolaudbrud fortsat ude af kontrol

segments.body: Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga survived Ebola and is sharing his experience to encourage people in eastern DR Congo to seek care. He says mistrust, threats and shortages complicate the response. In Butembo, samples must travel to another city for testing, a journey that can take 48 to 72 hours.

segments.title: A continuing emergency
segments.body: Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya says the outbreak remains uncontrolled six months after it was declared, citing scarce resources and attacks on health workers. The agency’s figures reported by Reuters put infections above 11,200 and deaths at 5,500. Kamwanga says healthcare workers also lack protective equipment.

perspectives.body: Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya warns that without bringing the outbreak under control, it could become the worst Ebola outbreak the world has seen.

content.headline: Fifth Canadian soldier dies after fire at military training base
content.shortHeadline: Fifth soldier dies after Canadian base fire
content.standfirst: Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco died a month after a fast-moving grass fire swept through a live-fire training area in Alberta. Four soldiers were killed initially and 24 military personnel remained in hospital as of Saturday.

image.caption: Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco died from injuries sustained in the fire.

sources.originalTitle: Fifth Canadian soldier dies from injuries caused by large fire at military base

segments.body: Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco died on Friday from injuries sustained when a grass fire spread across Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on 17 October. Four people were killed at the time, and 38 military personnel were injured, according to the Canadian Armed Forces.

segments.title: Investigation continues
segments.body: The fire broke out during a live-fire exercise and spread rapidly in strong winds. Officials said an investigation found it was likely sparked by a grenade launcher on the range. Firefighters could not tackle it immediately because the area may have contained unexploded ordnance.

content.headline: Australia’s gender-diverse sailors barred from US submarine training
content.shortHeadline: US policy bars gender-diverse Australians from submarine training
content.standfirst: Australian defence documents say transgender and non-binary personnel cannot begin the nuclear-submarine training pathway in the US, despite unchanged Australian inclusion policy. The restriction reflects US rules that apply to Australian personnel training there.

sources.originalTitle: Gender-diverse Australian sailors barred from US submarines despite Aukus deal, documents reveal

segments.body: Australian defence documents released under freedom-of-information laws say transgender and non-binary sailors and applicants cannot currently start the country’s nuclear-powered submarine training pathway. Australian personnel training in the US must comply with US policy, the briefing says.

segments.title: Training options
segments.body: Rear Adm Tish van Stralen said the navy was considering alternative career paths and possible training in the UK, whose policies she described as more liberal. Australia is preparing to buy US Virginia-class submarines, but the defence department did not say how many people have been affected.

content.headline: Ministers to discuss changing age-of-consent rules after Brand case
content.shortHeadline: Ministers to discuss age-of-consent change after Brand case
content.standfirst: Pat McFadden says a staggered age of consent will be discussed after a woman who alleges Russell Brand raped her when she was 16 called for adults to be barred from relationships with 16- and 17-year-olds. Her allegation was not part of his recent trial.

sources.originalTitle: Staggered age of consent to be discussed after Brand case, minister says

segments.body: Work and pensions secretary Pat McFadden says ministers will discuss proposals for a staggered age of consent. Mia Latter, who says she was 16 when she met Brand, is campaigning to make sexual relationships between adults and 16- and 17-year-olds illegal. Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault involving four other women; Latter’s allegation was not part of that trial.

segments.title: What is being proposed
segments.body: The campaign group Close the Consent Gap proposes that 16-year-olds could not have a sexual relationship with anyone over 19, and 17-year-olds with anyone over 20. The NSPCC says young people above the current age of consent can still be vulnerable to exploitation and are entitled to protection from harm.

content.headline: UK migrants face longer wait for settled status under new rules
content.shortHeadline: New rules extend settled-status wait for many migrants
content.standfirst: The standard qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain has risen from five to 10 years, with a shorter route for some higher earners and workers. Migrants interviewed by the i Paper say the change disrupts plans they made under the previous rules.

image.caption: Sarah Cohen says she is upset by the longer wait for settled status.

sources.originalTitle: Indefinite leave to remain changes are upsetting – I have to wait another seven years

segments.body: The government has doubled the standard qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain from five years to 10. The i Paper reports that people earning below £50,271 may now face the longer wait, while some higher earners and workers can qualify sooner. Time spent on a student visa does not count towards the period.

segments.title: People affected
segments.body: Sarah Cohen says the change adds seven years to her expected wait despite having been in the UK on a skilled-worker visa since 2023. Recent graduate Riley Connor says she is uncertain how she can afford the visa and NHS surcharge costs. The Home Office was approached for comment.

content.headline: Dover queue contingency sites cost £1.6m but were never used
content.shortHeadline: Unused Dover queue sites cost £1.6m
content.standfirst: Two emergency car parks built for possible delays from EU biometric checks were stood down after the expected summer queues did not materialise. The checks are still not operating for car passengers at Dover, and officials warn disruption could yet arise.

image.caption: A temporary vehicle-holding site was prepared for possible queues near Dover.

sources.originalTitle: EES farce as £1.6m spent turning race tracks into car parks – that were never used

segments.body: The Department for Transport says it spent £1.6m buying, converting and staffing two temporary vehicle-holding sites near Dover. They were intended to take cars off local roads if new Entry-Exit System checks caused severe queues, but both were stood down in August after the anticipated delays failed to occur.

segments.title: Checks still pending
segments.body: French biometric kiosks for car passengers at Dover have not been activated, and passengers are still being processed manually. The i Paper reports that the kiosks may not be ready until at least early 2027. Local leaders and MPs warn that full checks could still cause delays; the sites could be made available if traffic data suggests they are needed.

content.headline: UK and EU plan to share information on medicine shortages
content.shortHeadline: UK and EU plan medicine-shortage information sharing
content.standfirst: A proposed health-security agreement would let the UK and EU share information on shortages and sources of medicines including antibiotics, ADHD drugs and epilepsy treatments. The arrangement is expected to be discussed at the 20 November summit.

image.caption: Antibiotics on a production line at a pharmaceutical laboratory.

sources.originalTitle: Pharmacies to have better access to antibiotics and ADHD drugs in new Brexit deal

segments.body: A draft UK-EU statement describes a planned memorandum on health security and the sharing of information about medicine supplies. The agreement is expected to be welcomed at the Brussels summit on 20 November, but it has not yet been signed.

segments.title: Shortages continue
segments.body: The Nuffield Trust says earlier information could help identify available stocks and prevent shortages reaching patients. The report cites shortfalls affecting ADHD and epilepsy medicines, as well as Creon and Lanzoprazole. It says the planned cooperation may help manage current shortages and prepare for future ones.

content.headline: Fresh criticism at Venstre conference tests Poulsen’s green direction
content.shortHeadline: Venstre faces fresh dissent over Poulsen’s green direction
content.standfirst: The party leader received support at the weekend conference, but critics challenged the unclear meaning of Venstre’s “green journey” as proceedings ended. Troels Lund Poulsen must now turn the message into policy and rebuild support.

image.caption: Troels Lund Poulsen faced criticism as Venstre’s conference drew to a close.

sources.originalTitle: Efter forbrødning og fest kom der alligevel skår i den gode Venstre-stemning
Under de stående klapsalver ulmer uroen fortsat i Venstre - “Følg med, før an eller forsvind”
ANALYSE: Troels Lund fik partiets støtte, så han kan få vælgernes stemmer – ingen ved om det lykkes

segments.body: The closing debate at Venstre’s conference brought renewed criticism of the leadership’s green direction, despite applause for party leader Troels Lund Poulsen’s speech on Saturday. Critical farmer Asger Krogsgaard won a place on the party’s executive board, and delegates questioned the lack of detail about the “green journey” and the party’s campaign line.

segments.title: Policy will be the test
segments.body: DR’s analysis says Poulsen has tied his leadership to establishing green credibility and winning back voters, but the result is uncertain. Upcoming decisions, including pesticide restrictions and compensation for farmers, will test whether the party can translate that direction into policy.

perspectives.body: DR’s analysis argues that the test is not just whether Venstre adopts a greener profile, but whether voters reward it and whether the party can sustain that credibility through concrete decisions.

content.headline: Denmark’s Supreme Court may rule on disputed housing-list criterion
content.shortHeadline: Supreme Court may assess disputed housing-list criterion
content.standfirst: A case over 91 lease terminations in Helsingør could lead the court to assess whether classifying areas partly by residents’ non-Western background is discriminatory. A decision is expected on 23 November; no ruling has yet been made.

image.caption: Nøjsomhed in Helsingør, an area included on the government’s housing list.

sources.originalTitle: Snart et år efter EU-dom: Nu tyder meget på, at Højesteret vil vurdere, om omstridt ghettokriterie diskriminerer

segments.body: Seven Supreme Court judges have heard arguments in a case over 91 lease terminations in the Nøjsomhed housing area in Helsingør. The tenants’ lawyer argues that using the share of residents with a non-Western background in the “parallel society” criteria breaches the ban on ethnic discrimination. The landlord disputes the challenge.

segments.title: A wider legal question
segments.body: The European Court of Justice has said the criterion may constitute discrimination, but left the final assessment to Danish courts. The report says a Supreme Court decision on 23 November could affect other cases; it remains possible that the judges will decide only the Helsingør dispute.

content.headline: Police record more cases of children breaking e-scooter rules
content.shortHeadline: E-scooter rule-breaking cases among children rise sharply
content.standfirst: Police figures cited by insurer If show cases involving 10- to 16-year-olds rose 128% to 701 in 2025, with more recorded so far this year. The rise may partly reflect increased police attention, and safety groups want the trial rules for small electric vehicles ended.

sources.originalTitle: Sager med børn på elløbehjul eksploderer

segments.body: Cases involving 10- to 16-year-olds breaking traffic rules on e-scooters and similar vehicles rose 128% between 2024 and 2025, to 701, according to police figures cited by insurer If. If says more cases have already been recorded in 2026 than in the whole of last year.

segments.title: Safety concerns
segments.body: If says the increase may partly reflect greater police attention, while hospitals have also reported more e-scooter injuries. The Traffic Safety Think Tank argues that the trial arrangements allowing these vehicles on cycle paths should end. A 2025 Transport Authority evaluation found police-recorded injury risk on e-scooters was eight to nine times that for bicycles.

content.headline: Nearly two million Danes have recorded an organ-donation decision
content.shortHeadline: Nearly two million Danes have recorded organ-donation choices
content.standfirst: The number of Danes who have registered a decision is at its highest level, with nearly two million nationwide, according to the Danish Center for Organ Donation. The report explains that adults must still actively confirm their wishes.

sources.originalTitle: Nyt hjerte gav hende livet tilbage – nu har rekordmange taget stilling

segments.body: Annelise Buhl Staunstrup received a heart transplant in 2014 after being diagnosed with serious heart disease. Her experience comes as nearly two million people across Denmark have recorded an organ-donation decision, the highest number to date, according to the Danish Center for Organ Donation.

segments.title: A decision still needs confirming
segments.body: Under a law that took effect in June 2025, adults are entered in the organ-donor register by default, but the record is not confirmed until they actively choose an option. If a person has not recorded a confirmed decision, relatives may be asked to decide after their death.

content.headline: EU climate chief cites Denmark as a model ahead of COP31 talks
content.shortHeadline: EU climate chief cites Denmark’s green-energy model
content.standfirst: Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra says Europe must push harder at COP31 as it warms faster than other continents. He points to Denmark’s climate goals and renewable-energy business as an example for others to follow.

image.caption: EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra negotiates at COP31 in Türkiye.

sources.originalTitle: Klimaboss er ikke i tvivl om Europas rolle: 'Vi er nødt til at spille hårdere og tale højere'

segments.body: EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra says the bloc should press for greater emissions cuts and stronger protection against heat and flooding at the UN climate talks in Türkiye. He says Europe needs to speak more forcefully as extreme weather intensifies and the US has withdrawn from the Paris climate agreement.

segments.title: A Danish example
segments.body: Hoekstra describes Denmark’s ambitious climate targets and renewable-energy sector, particularly wind power, as a model for Europe. He argues that climate policy is also about economic resilience and reducing reliance on imported fossil fuels.

content.headline: EU forces board tanker suspected of belonging to Russia’s shadow fleet
content.shortHeadline: EU forces board suspected Russian shadow-fleet tanker
content.standfirst: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas says a Mediterranean operation found the tanker MV MIDAG was sailing under a false flag. Denmark’s straits are a key route for Russian shadow-fleet vessels.

image.caption: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas in Dublin.

sources.originalTitle: Kallas: EU-styrker har bordet mistænkt skyggetanker

segments.body: EU naval forces boarded the tanker MV MIDAG in the Mediterranean on 13 November, according to EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas. She says the inspection, carried out under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, confirmed that the vessel was sailing under a false flag.

segments.title: A route through Danish waters
segments.body: The EU says it will continue efforts to disrupt Russia’s shadow fleet, which helps fund its invasion of Ukraine, and plans further sanctions. The report notes that Russian shadow-fleet vessels use the Danish straits to reach the open sea from ports including St Petersburg.

content.headline: Carmelle wins the first Eurovision Asia contest for the Philippines
content.shortHeadline: Carmelle takes the first Eurovision Asia win for the Philippines
content.standfirst: The 19-year-old singer’s pop-rap entry, “Sobra-Sobra”, topped the jury and public votes in Bangkok. The debut contest brought 11 countries together for a regional spin on Eurovision.

image.caption: Carmelle performs “Sobra-Sobra” at the Eurovision Asia grand final in Bangkok.

sources.originalTitle: Philippines’ Carmelle wins first Eurovision contest in Asia

segments.body: Carmelle Collado, performing as Carmelle, won the inaugural Eurovision Asia contest in Bangkok with “Sobra-Sobra”. The Philippines’ entry scored 211 points, finishing 41 ahead of host country Thailand; Vietnam came third. Carmelle received the most votes from both the national juries and the public ballot.

segments.title: A new regional stage
segments.body: The song blends pop and rap with traditional Philippine instruments, the kubing and kulintang, and is sung in Tagalog and English. Carmelle said it celebrates female empowerment and is “a tribute to all Filipino women”. Organisers say future editions will not automatically go to the winning country, citing the infrastructure smaller countries would need to host.

content.headline: U2’s Carnaval De Luz finds renewed joy, though not every song lands
content.shortHeadline: U2 return to form on Carnaval De Luz, with some unevenness
content.standfirst: The band’s first album of original material in nearly a decade reconnects with its expansive sound. One review hears a career-best record in years; another finds its strongest moments in the band’s renewed chemistry, but notes uneven writing.

image.caption: U2 have kept the same line-up throughout their long career.

sources.originalTitle: U2 lost the plot decades ago – their new album finally fixes that
Carnaval De Luz

segments.body: U2’s first album of original material since 2017, Carnaval De Luz, reaches for open-hearted songs about community, hope and healing. The i Paper review hears the band reconnecting with its melodic strengths and calls it their best album in 25 years, while acknowledging that it lacks a unifying hit and sometimes overreaches.

perspectives.body: The i Paper sees the record as a substantial return to form, while questioning whether it can restore U2’s wider commercial relevance in a fragmented pop landscape.

segments.title: A band looking inward
segments.body: Pitchfork places the record’s renewed spark in the band’s reduced, more collaborative sound, following drummer Larry Mullen Jr’s neck injury and the return of the original four members to making music together. It praises the opening and closing run, but finds the middle less assured and suggests stronger songs from the earlier EPs might have helped.

perspectives.body: Pitchfork frames the album less as a bid to reclaim past stature than as a reflection on longevity, friendship and the band’s renewed connection after Mullen’s injury.

content.headline: Paris Paloma’s arena-scale show turns feminist anger into shared release
content.shortHeadline: Paris Paloma turns feminist fury into arena-scale pop
content.standfirst: At Bristol Beacon, the singer paired songs from her second album with dramatic staging and a crowd already embracing unreleased material. The review sees a performance built for larger rooms without losing its communal spirit.

image.caption: Paris Paloma performs at Bristol Beacon.

sources.originalTitle: Paris Paloma review – arena-scale alt-pop drama from a singer on her way to bigger things

segments.body: Paris Paloma’s Bristol show suggested a step towards bigger venues: the crowd danced to an unreleased song, “Fairy Dance”, written about the community around her music. Onstage, a sculpture inspired by Ithell Colquhoun’s Tree of Veins and wind machines amplified the theatrical scale of songs from The Fatal Flaw.

segments.title: Anger and connection
segments.body: The set moves between feminist fury and more reflective material. “Good Girl” directs its anger at tech bros and manosphere influencers; “Rothko” turns a teenage encounter with art into a quieter meditation. The review argues that Paloma’s accessible melodies help her make a case for creativity and community without disguising the seriousness of her concerns.

content.headline: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul turn grief and parenthood into new pop
content.shortHeadline: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul make a more personal album
content.standfirst: The Belgian duo’s second album, Mainland Madinina, draws on bereavement, family life and a writing trip to Martinique. Their playful pop still makes room for satire, but its centre has shifted towards vulnerability.

image.caption: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Would you breastfeed your own father?’ The goofy, spiky world of art-pop duo Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul

segments.body: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul’s forthcoming album, Mainland Madinina, grows out of losses both have experienced: Pupul’s mother died between records, as did Adigéry’s father, who had Alzheimer’s. The duo went to Martinique, where Adigéry’s parents are from, and began with stripped-back demos that became a more introspective collection.

segments.title: Humour with a deeper undertow
segments.body: The record retains the duo’s comic edge, including on “Googoo Gaga” and “From Healer to Dealer”, a send-up of wellness culture and therapy language. But songs about raising children and processing grief take the album in a more intimate direction. Adigéry describes parenthood as a mirror for thinking about what people inherit and what they want to leave behind.

content.headline: Armand Hammer’s Snakes & Ladders turns everyday life into political art
content.shortHeadline: Armand Hammer make hard times the subject of Snakes & Ladders
content.standfirst: billy woods and Elucid build their latest album from fragmented observations, inventive production and a close-knit circle of collaborators. The review hears political force in its difficult, deliberately unresolved songs.

sources.originalTitle: Snakes & Ladders

segments.body: On the surprise-released Snakes & Ladders, Armand Hammer turn ordinary places and encounters into dense, sharply observed writing. The review singles out “Jet Magazine” and “Send for Me” for drawing wider histories and political unease out of streets and neighbourhood details.

segments.title: A community of sound
segments.body: Producers including clipping., Preservation, Kenny Segal and Child Actor contribute to a record whose varied beats still feel cohesive. The review argues that its fractured form suits the material: these are not easy times, and the songs make room for anxiety, memory and the work of imagining something better.

content.headline: Krill return after 11 years with a more reflective Secret Language
content.shortHeadline: Krill return with new perspective on Secret Language
content.standfirst: The Boston indie-rock cult favourites reunite with an album shaped by time apart, new lives and a changed sound. The review finds their old anxious humour alongside a newly tender and hopeful streak.

sources.originalTitle: Secret Language

segments.body: Secret Language is Krill’s first album in 11 years. The band split in 2015 after singer and bassist Jonah Furman felt he had run out of things to say; in the intervening years, members took on work in areas including labour organising, public housing and civil-rights law. The review hears the reunion as a reassessment rather than a simple return.

New guitar textures, harmonies, violin and saxophone soften the band’s familiar anxious indie rock. Furman still writes about self-doubt and injustice, but also about family, commitment and love. The review finds the record’s closing message unexpectedly hopeful: that people can build something better even when the world remains unfair.

content.headline: Eris Drew and Octo Octa make dance music from their New Hampshire cabin
content.shortHeadline: Eris Drew and Octo Octa turn their cabin into a dance studio
content.standfirst: Their first collaborative album draws on vintage dance records, psych-folk instruments and the maximalism of 1990s big beat. The review finds its most affecting moment in a warm, comparatively unreferential song about home.

sources.originalTitle: Alchemical Sisters

segments.body: For Alchemical Sisters, Eris Drew and Octo Octa transformed a bedroom in their New Hampshire cabin into a studio, building tracks from synths, psych-folk instruments and samples from their vintage dance archive. The review hears the result as a maximalist, playful take on the 1990s big-beat sound.

segments.title: A song about home
segments.body: The album’s samples and references are part of its character, but the review singles out “Song for New Hampshire” as its emotional centre: a warmly personal track that leans less on borrowed sounds. Its earnestness, the critic suggests, helps explain the creative partnership’s sense of shared purpose.

content.headline: Wicker’s kinky fairy tale is funny, troubling and hard to pin down
content.shortHeadline: Wicker is a bawdy fairy tale with a troubling gender flip
content.standfirst: Olivia Colman plays a woman who commissions a husband made of willow, in a comedy that invites both laughter and questions about agency. The review finds its sexism hard to ignore, while the filmmakers and a scholar place it in a wider tradition of monster romance.

image.caption: Olivia Colman as the Fisherwoman with the husband made of wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it
A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker

segments.body: In Wicker, a Fisherwoman played by Olivia Colman pays a basketmaker, played by Peter Dinklage, to make her a husband. Alexander Skarsgård’s willow-built creation is devoted to her, and the village is unsettled by their relationship. The review enjoys the film’s bawdy absurdity but sees a deliberate gender reversal that leaves the husband’s wishes largely unexplored.

perspectives.body: The BBC feature places Wicker in the monster-romance tradition, where desire and difference can challenge social expectations. Its filmmakers connect the premise to domestic labour and the scrutiny women face in dating, while a scholar notes the genre’s appeal to audiences drawn to overlooked outsiders.

segments.title: Fantasy and power
segments.body: The i Paper review ultimately embraces the film as an impossible fairy tale rather than a relationship model, and finds a simple argument beneath the excess: women want partners who treat them as equals. It also notes how the story’s extra material gives the Tailor’s Wife, a character barely present in the original short story, her own frustration and desire for agency.

content.headline: Robert Pattinson is reportedly a leading contender to play James Bond
content.shortHeadline: Robert Pattinson emerges as a Bond contender, reports say
content.standfirst: A report says Amazon MGM has offered the actor more favourable terms than other candidates, suggesting the studio may prefer a recognisable star. No casting decision has been announced.

image.caption: Robert Pattinson has reportedly been offered a larger fee in his test deal.

sources.originalTitle: Robert Pattinson reportedly leads James Bond contenders
‘It was a train wreck! I was terrified’: how the new James Bond will be announced – and what can go wrong

segments.body: Robert Pattinson has emerged as a possible favourite to succeed Daniel Craig as James Bond, according to a report by Puck’s Matthew Belloni. The report says Pattinson’s test deal calls for three films rather than four and a larger, unspecified fee than those offered to other actors. The studio has not confirmed its choice.

segments.title: A high-profile casting process
segments.body: The Guardian’s account of previous Bond announcements describes a franchise under new ownership, with Amazon MGM holding creative control, Denis Villeneuve directing and Steven Knight writing. It also recalls how the publicity around Daniel Craig’s introduction went awry, a reminder that the next announcement will carry its own risks as well as signalling the series’ direction.

perspectives.body: The Guardian focuses on the staging of the announcement itself, tracing how Bond unveilings have shifted from trade notices to high-pressure public events—and why a leak can make that moment harder to control.

content.headline: Ebenezer gives Johnny Depp a decent Scrooge, but redemption is less convincing
content.shortHeadline: Johnny Depp makes a stronger Scrooge before redemption
content.standfirst: The new A Christmas Carol adaptation gives Depp room to play a petulant, bad-tempered miser, though the review finds less depth in his transformation. A separate account examines how the film is being positioned as part of the actor’s Hollywood comeback.

image.caption: Johnny Depp as Scrooge in Ebenezer.

sources.originalTitle: Ebenezer review – Johnny Depp’s Scrooge tries to exorcise ghosts of business past
'Cancelled' star Johnny Depp is making a big Hollywood comeback - will it succeed?

segments.body: Ti West’s version of A Christmas Carol follows the familiar story but adds a prologue in which Jacob Marley, played by Ian McKellen, is still alive, as well as changes to Scrooge’s past. The Guardian review finds Johnny Depp convincing as the miser—especially before his change of heart—but says the redeemed Scrooge lacks some of the ending’s pathos.

perspectives.body: The BBC examines the film’s release as a test of Depp’s Hollywood return, setting supportive audience reactions beside criticism of the comeback-focused publicity and expert views on how audiences respond to the actor.

segments.body: The BBC’s reporting notes that Depp was dropped from Fantastic Beasts after losing a UK libel case, then won a separate US case brought against Amber Heard. It also reports that the film’s publicity stresses his return while offering little access to Depp and West. Those competing views leave the meaning of “comeback” unresolved.

content.headline: This week’s cinema releases bring Cynthia Erivo, Johnny Depp and a new Scrooge
content.shortHeadline: This week in cinemas: Erivo, Depp and a new Scrooge
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s release roundup ranges from Cynthia Erivo’s courtroom drama Prima Facie to documentaries, international films and Johnny Depp’s Ebenezer. Its quick verdicts help readers navigate a crowded week of cinema.

image.caption: A selection of this week’s film releases, including Johnny Depp in Ebenezer and Cynthia Erivo in Prima Facie.

sources.originalTitle: Guilty or redeemed? Our critics’ verdicts on this week’s UK cinema releases

segments.body: Among the week’s releases, the Guardian highlights Prima Facie, with Cynthia Erivo as a lawyer whose work defending rape suspects is complicated by experience, and a documentary about filmmaker David Wilkinson’s bowel-cancer treatment. The roundup also points to a phone-filmed account of an Iranian refugee’s journey and a film about Vietnam’s first Black special operations team.

For lighter or more familiar viewing, the roundup praises Johnny Depp’s performance as Scrooge in Ebenezer and notes a tennis documentary about Billie Jean King. It also includes a Chinese forensic-science thriller, a Second World War drama and films ranging from Ran to David Bowie’s The Man Who Fell to Earth.

content.headline: Renate Reinsve looks back on the role that nearly came too late
content.shortHeadline: Renate Reinsve on the film role that changed her career
content.standfirst: Reinsve thought she would leave acting before Joachim Trier offered her the lead in The Worst Person in the World. She recalls the film’s collaborative shoot and discusses the very different challenge of playing a mother in Fjord.

sources.originalTitle: 'It stopped me quitting acting': Renate Reinsve on her life-changing role in The Worst Person in the World

segments.body: Renate Reinsve was considering leaving acting when Joachim Trier called with the lead role in The Worst Person in the World. The film’s success changed her career, but she remembers the shoot itself as a playful summer in Oslo and says she recognised something of herself in Julie, its restless heroine.

segments.title: A different kind of performance
segments.body: In Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord, Reinsve plays Lisbet, a quiet evangelical Christian whose family faces accusations of abusing their children. Reinsve says she was drawn to finding compassion for a character unlike herself. She also welcomes the film’s refusal to dictate what audiences should think about its conflict over family and religious beliefs.

content.headline: Honey’s cold-war spy comedy charms, though its early promise fades
content.shortHeadline: Honey is a stylish spy comedy that loses some early spark
content.standfirst: Two reviews admire the series’ wit, visual flair and Ann Skelly’s young spy, while differing on how much its playful style undermines its East Berlin setting. Both find plenty of entertainment in the show’s irreverent approach.

image.caption: Ann Skelly stars as Martha in Honey.

sources.originalTitle: Honey review – a hugely entertaining Killing Eve prequel that’s packed with naughty jokes
Honey: this flirty, kinky Killing Eve prequel should have been called Carré on Spying

segments.body: Honey follows Martha, a young British agent in 1980s East Berlin, where her assignments include seducing men and gathering compromising photographs. The Guardian review praises Ann Skelly’s confidence, the show’s period styling and its comic inventions, but says the season settles into familiar thriller rhythms and makes Martha’s initial defiance less convincing.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s other review is more sceptical about the historical setting: it sees a knowingly camp, pop-fuelled comedy rather than convincing Cold War espionage, and argues that the show’s interest is in style, banter and kink.

segments.title: Entertainment over realism
segments.body: Both reviews find the show entertaining, but the second argues its knowingly anachronistic jokes and glamorous heroine make the East German setting a playful backdrop rather than a convincing portrait of an oppressed society. The first likewise notes that the Killing Eve connection is largely a label, not a close match in tone.

content.headline: Ade Adepitan on joining I’m a Celebrity as its first wheelchair user
content.shortHeadline: Ade Adepitan on making I’m a Celebrity accessible
content.standfirst: The Paralympian and presenter says he helped producers plan access for his first jungle appearance. He also discusses the backlash to his casting, and why the opportunity matters beyond his own participation.

image.caption: Ade Adepitan, who is set to appear on I’m a Celebrity.

sources.originalTitle: ‘You can’t train to be chucked in a box full of rats!’ Ade Adepitan on fear, facing down sharks and being I’m a Celeb’s first wheelchair user

segments.body: Ade Adepitan is set to become the first wheelchair user on I’m a Celebrity, Get Me Out of Here!. He visited the camp to advise producers on accessibility, including its changing terrain and narrow paths. He says that needing different mobility aids is not an advantage: “Being disabled is like starting a race … five miles behind anyone else.”

segments.title: Visibility and barriers
segments.body: Adepitan says he hopes taking part will prompt discussion about disability, after his casting drew online accusations of “cheating” and claims that a disabled person should not be on a primetime show. He describes the barriers of everyday life—from broken station lifts to taxi refusals—and says the disabling force is often the physical and social obstacles society chooses to create.

content.headline: The week’s TV picks include a crypto drama and Yellowjackets’ final season
content.shortHeadline: This week on TV: The Altruists and Yellowjackets return
content.standfirst: A streaming guide weighs up dramas inspired by FTX and the opioid crisis, the final Yellowjackets season and a Belfast comedy about care work. It also flags a Melania Trump documentary follow-up and a new run of The Chosen.

image.caption: Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison and Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

sources.originalTitle: The Altruists to Yellowjackets: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The Guardian’s picks include Netflix drama The Altruists, about Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, and the final season of Yellowjackets. The guide finds the crypto series somewhat staid, but says its story of tech idealists and risk-taking feels timely; it is less sure whether Yellowjackets can bring its tangled timelines to a satisfying close.

Other options include Rewarding, a quieter BBC comedy-drama about under-resourced Belfast care workers, and The Hotline, a documentary following volunteers who support people at risk of overdose. The selection also features a new run of The Chosen, a two-episode Melania Trump follow-up and family fantasy Percy Jackson and the Olympians.

content.headline: Tonight’s TV: an undercover look at Crowborough’s asylum camp
content.shortHeadline: Tonight: Inside the Asylum Camp and Blue Planet III
content.standfirst: The evening guide leads with a documentary filmed inside the Crowborough asylum camp, described as a bleak account of conditions and community responses. It also recommends wildlife, drama and music across the schedule.

image.caption: Inside the Asylum Camp, the documentary about the Crowborough facility.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: a tough look inside Crowborough asylum camp

segments.body: Inside the Asylum Camp goes undercover at the former military facility in Crowborough, now housing asylum seekers. The Guardian’s guide describes it as a sad, balanced documentary about traumatised residents and locals whose responses range from ignorance to generosity, and says the situation could be better for everyone.

The evening’s other suggestions include Blue Planet III, featuring seasonal wildlife behaviour; a new episode of the Belfast crime drama; a fishing trip on the River Tees; and an intimate Later… performance by Dublin rockers. The guide also recommends the film Conclave.

content.headline: I’m a Celebrity’s new line-up makes a case for less controversy
content.shortHeadline: I’m a Celebrity swaps political flashpoints for a friendly cast
content.standfirst: The i Paper argues that the show’s new campmates are a welcome change from politicians who used past series to rehabilitate their reputations. It says a more companionable group can make better viewing, even without the same headline-grabbing conflict.

image.caption: Ant and Dec return to present I’m a Celebrity.

sources.originalTitle: I’m a Celeb has finally learned its lesson

segments.body: The i Paper’s column welcomes a line-up led by Wayne Rooney, alongside figures including Ricky Wilson, Joanna Page, AJ Odudu and Ade Adepitan. It contrasts them with former contestants Nigel Farage and Matt Hancock, arguing that their stints helped soften the public image of divisive political figures.

The writer questions whether reality TV needs controversial contestants to create drama, and points to the previous year’s calmer series as evidence that viewers can enjoy campmates getting along and sharing their stories. The hope is that this year’s cast will make amiability entertaining rather than dull.

content.headline: Maya Jama’s next move tests whether TV can still make a new star
content.shortHeadline: Can Netflix give Maya Jama a show to match her star power?
content.standfirst: After leaving Love Island and signing a Netflix deal, Jama has a larger audience but an uncertain next step. The column argues that established presenting slots are scarce and a new format is hard to make succeed.

image.caption: Maya Jama is leaving Love Island after nine series.

sources.originalTitle: Maya Jama belongs to a dying breed of presenters

segments.body: Maya Jama is leaving Love Island after nine series and has signed a deal with Netflix, where several projects are in development. The i Paper argues that her profile has grown through work including the Brit Awards and Celebrity Traitors, even as the dating show has lost some of its cultural prominence.

segments.title: A difficult path to the next format
segments.body: The column sees a crowded field of established presenters and few major programmes ready for a new host. It suggests Netflix could give Jama room to build something of her own, but notes that making a new format catch on is difficult. The projects themselves have not yet been announced.

content.headline: Patricia Hodge on Miranda, playing Thatcher and becoming a mother at 42
content.shortHeadline: Patricia Hodge looks back on a life in comedy and drama
content.standfirst: The actor discusses her comic reputation, playing Margaret Thatcher and the long wait to have children. She also reflects on how Miranda helped women embrace silliness and shares why her newer role in Marble Hall Murders keeps her in the public eye.

image.caption: Patricia Hodge, whose television roles include Miranda and Marble Hall Murders.

sources.originalTitle: Patricia Hodge on conceiving at 45: ‘It was a test of endurance’

segments.body: Patricia Hodge recalls the comedy she found on stage and in Miranda, where she played Penny, a high-status mother repeatedly undone by her daughter’s chaotic humour. She believes the sitcom helped women feel more able to laugh at themselves, and describes how an early habit of breaking into laughter onstage eventually became something she learned to control.

Hodge also discusses playing Margaret Thatcher without imitating her voice, and how she drew on the contrast between public and private life. She had her first child at 42 after a difficult journey to conceive and her second at 45; the interview finds her delighted by the arrival of a new grandson.

content.headline: GTA VI’s launch hype overshadows a dispute over dismissed workers
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s hype and the labour dispute behind its launch
content.standfirst: A hands-on preview shows Rockstar’s most detailed Grand Theft Auto yet, built around a criminal couple and more deliberate play. A separate report questions viral claims about mass workplace absences and highlights a tribunal case brought by dismissed staff.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto VI brings Jason and Lucia into a new crime story set in fictional Florida.

sources.originalTitle: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
‘Grand Theft Auto Flu’: is the whole world really taking the day off work to play GTA VI?

segments.body: Grand Theft Auto VI takes players to a fictional Florida and follows Jason and Lucia, a criminal couple whose relationship players can shape. Rockstar’s demonstration reveals a world dense with activity and detail, while its developers say the game encourages planning crimes and avoiding indiscriminate violence without removing player freedom.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s separate report questions claims that GTA VI will cause a billion-dollar productivity hit. It says the figure lacks hard data and argues that coverage of “GTA Flu” has pushed a more concrete employment dispute out of view.

segments.title: The people behind the release
segments.body: Rockstar says it fired 34 employees in the UK and Canada for leaking confidential information; the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain says the dismissals were union-busting. Former developer Will Mesilane says his dismissal disrupted his life and believes it was linked to his union involvement. The Glasgow tribunal’s closing submissions are scheduled for 17 and 18 November, just before the game’s release.

content.headline: Artists use satirical games to challenge Trump administration propaganda
content.shortHeadline: Satirical games turn political propaganda back on Trump
content.standfirst: Independent creators have made games that parody the White House’s own political arcade and its treatment of immigration, war and corruption. Their projects use familiar formats to make political messaging playable—and harder to ignore.

image.caption: The Secret Handshake’s satirical game Operation Epic Furious.

sources.originalTitle: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda

segments.body: After the White House launched browser games promoting its policies, artists and developers made satirical alternatives. The Secret Handshake’s Operation Epic Furious: Strait to Hell asks players to control Donald Trump and choose between ordering a Diet Coke and invading Iran; it is deliberately unwinnable. The collective says the administration’s use of games to promote war prompted its response.

segments.title: Games as political language
segments.body: Other projects recast Space Invaders and Donkey Kong to criticise issues including healthcare cuts, political corruption and rising fuel prices. The creators range from game developers to advertising workers with no previous design experience. The feature reports that more than 350,000 people have played The Secret Handshake’s games online.

content.headline: The Ocarina of Time remake brings fans back for a midnight launch
content.shortHeadline: Zelda fans queue at midnight for Ocarina of Time
content.standfirst: Hundreds gathered on Oxford Street for a physical copy of the Switch 2 remake and exclusive collectibles. The writer’s long wait begins as a celebration of shared fandom but ends with practical frustrations.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?

segments.body: The release of a lavish 4K remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time drew about 500 fans to an Oxford Street midnight launch. The writer joined them for a game copy, an ocarina-shaped keyring and a replica of the original Nintendo 64 box—an increasingly unusual chance to experience a launch as a shared event.

segments.title: Nostalgia meets a long queue
segments.body: The queue took hours, and the shop was still out of reach when it closed; staff asked remaining customers to leave their details so the collectible box could be posted later. The writer’s enthusiasm gives way to doubts about the wait, but the gathering still offers a glimpse of the communal side of gaming in an age of digital downloads.

content.headline: Can Alex Garland make Elden Ring work as a Hollywood fantasy film?
content.shortHeadline: Elden Ring’s film adaptation faces a world-building challenge
content.standfirst: The game’s vast, grotesque fantasy setting and reported $200m budget raise familiar questions about adapting an intricate world for cinema. The feature considers what the film might draw from and why its director’s track record offers no guarantee.

image.caption: Artwork from Elden Ring, the fantasy game being adapted by Alex Garland.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is on course to be Hollywood’s goriest ever fantasy movie

segments.body: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is reportedly shot and in post-production, with a cast including Cailee Spaeny, Ben Whishaw and Nick Offerman. The film’s reported budget is close to $200m, and its source material is known for a bleak, horror-inflected world rather than a conventional heroic fantasy.

segments.title: A world is not a story
segments.body: The feature warns that earlier fantasy adaptations have stumbled by diluting their source material or assuming audiences will care about world-building alone. Leaked images have prompted speculation that Garland might draw on events before the game begins, but the story’s direction and how much creative freedom he will have remain unknown.

content.headline: Starship makes first tower catch of its upper stage, despite booster loss
content.shortHeadline: Starship catches upper stage; booster lost
content.standfirst: SpaceX’s upper stage returned to its Texas launch tower after orbiting Earth 14 times, the first time the company has caught that part of the rocket. The booster diverted and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico.

image.caption: SpaceX’s Starship upper stage returns to the launch tower after an orbital test flight.

sources.originalTitle: SpaceX’s Starship returns to launch pad from orbit in victory for company

segments.body: SpaceX caught Starship’s 171ft upper stage in the mechanical arms of its Texas launch tower on Saturday, after a 22-hour mission that circled Earth 14 times. It was the first successful tower catch of the upper stage and only the second time Starship has entered orbit.

segments.title: A partial success
segments.body: The planned double catch failed when the Super Heavy booster diverted after launch and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX said its guidance system had detected that the booster was out of position for a catch; the company’s chief executive, Elon Musk, also said it was slightly low on fuel.

segments.title: Why it matters
segments.body: The test is a step towards SpaceX’s goal of making the vehicle rapidly reusable, and comes as Nasa’s planned 2028 return of humans to the Moon approaches. Starship also deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites on this flight. The company has discussed increasing test flights to a weekly, then twice-weekly, pace.

content.headline: Medical micro-robots show promise delivering drugs in pigs and blood vessels
content.shortHeadline: Micro-robots target drugs inside the body
content.standfirst: Researchers are testing magnetically guided devices that could deliver medicines to precise locations. The work remains experimental: one device delivered insulin in pigs, while another was tested in a model of the brain’s circulation.

image.caption: Illustration of a magnetic micro-robot designed to deliver medicine inside the gut.

sources.originalTitle: The astonishing micro-robots you swallow that spot cancer and might help treat it

segments.body: A 6.5mm magnetic “spiny milli-ball” developed in Beijing carried insulin to the lower intestine of pigs in a test reported this month. Its casing dissolves after swallowing, and its spikes help pull the device into gut tissue, where it releases the drug. The research is not evidence that the device is ready for patient use.

segments.title: From the gut to blood vessels
segments.body: Other researchers are testing smaller devices for movement through blood vessels. A team at ETH Zürich guided a 2mm robot through a pig’s bloodstream using magnets and X-ray imaging. In a separate silicone model of the brain’s circulation, it delivered a drug designed to dissolve a clot.

perspectives.body: Roboticist Bradley Nelson argues that precise delivery could reduce the amount of a drug needed and, potentially, limit toxicity. Those are prospective benefits, not results established in patients.

segments.title: A long road to clinical use
segments.body: The report describes these systems as research-stage technology. Devices small enough to travel through human blood vessels are likely to be years from patient use, while swallowable camera capsules are already used to investigate some gut problems. Possible future applications include treating tumours, infections and blood clots.

content.headline: Small study raises hope a blood-pressure drug could have lasting effects
content.shortHeadline: Could a blood-pressure pill have lasting effects?
content.standfirst: Follow-up of 14 patients taking baxdrostat found that their blood pressure remained lower after they stopped the drug, in some cases for up to two years. Researchers say a larger study is needed before calling the effect a cure.

sources.originalTitle: New drug that could permanently cure high blood pressure coming to UK by 2027

segments.body: Baxdrostat is designed to reduce production of aldosterone, a hormone that can raise blood pressure. An analysis of a larger drug trial followed 14 patients who had responded strongly: after taking the medicine for six to 12 months, they stopped, and their blood pressure remained lower during follow-up of up to two years.

segments.title: A possibility, not a proven cure
segments.body: The researchers suggest the drug may also damage cells that overproduce aldosterone in some benign adrenal tumours, which can cause hypertension. The result could offer an alternative to surgery for some patients, but the small follow-up cannot establish that the effect is permanent. The study’s researchers say a larger trial is under way.

perspectives.body: Morris Brown, a study investigator, said longer follow-up might support a claim that a finite course of treatment can produce a lasting cure, but stressed that a larger study is needed to prove it.

content.headline: Blood test detects ovarian cancer precursor in early study
content.shortHeadline: Blood test flags ovarian cancer precursor
content.standfirst: Researchers report that a blood signal called Tu-Stroma identified a precursor lesion in most affected women in their study. The finding is promising, but the report does not establish that the test is ready for routine screening.

image.caption: Illustration of the fallopian-tube lining, where ovarian cancer precursor changes can begin.

sources.originalTitle: Molecular signal in blood helps detect early risk for ovarian cancer, study finds

segments.body: Researchers measured levels of an RNA molecule called Tu-Stroma in blood and reported detecting serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma, a precursor condition associated with ovarian cancer, in 92.3% of affected women. The test correctly identified 98.2% of healthy women in the study.

segments.title: What remains to be shown
segments.body: The researchers say the signal could eventually help identify risk before invasive cancer develops, including for women with inherited risk factors who face difficult decisions about preventive surgery. The report presents a potential diagnostic approach, not evidence that using it improves outcomes or is suitable for general screening.

content.headline: South Korean top exam scorer admits using AI and hidden camera to cheat
content.shortHeadline: Top South Korean exam scorer admits AI cheating
content.standfirst: The candidate said he photographed test questions with a miniature camera, sent them to an AI tool and checked the answers on a phone. His admission has raised concerns days before South Korea’s high-stakes college entrance exam.

image.caption: Han Won-seok confesses to cheating in a video posted on his lawyer’s YouTube channel.

sources.originalTitle: 160 questions, only one wrong: top scorer in South Korea tax exam admits AI cheating
South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating

segments.body: A candidate who ranked first in both rounds of South Korea’s tax-accountant qualification exam admitted using a hidden camera, a smartphone and generative AI to cheat. He said he photographed questions, sent them to an AI tool and checked its answers on his phone. He had scored 397.5 out of 400 in the first round.

segments.title: Investigation and consequences
segments.body: Han, identified by surname in his confession, submitted a written admission to Seoul police after initially denying wrongdoing. The government says people found to have used AI to cheat in the exam will lose their qualification and be barred from retaking it for five years. Officials are considering countermeasures before the national college entrance exam.

perspectives.body: The BBC reports that the government has announced qualification revocation and a five-year ban for exam candidates found to have cheated using AI; police have assigned Han’s case to investigators.

content.headline: Tesla offers Cybercab for private use, with a $299 monthly fee
content.shortHeadline: Tesla’s Cybercab offer comes with a $299 monthly fee
content.standfirst: Invited buyers in limited service areas can place deposits on Tesla’s steering-wheel-free robotaxi, but it is restricted to geofenced locations and requires a monthly autonomy subscription. A US safety audit is still under way.

sources.originalTitle: Tesla is inviting some people to buy a Cybercab ‘for personal use’ — but read the fine print
Tesla opens Cybercab pre-orders ‘for personal use,’ with geo restrictions and a $299 monthly fee

segments.body: Tesla has invited some customers to order a Cybercab for personal use, listing a price of $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly autonomy fee. Initial availability is limited to supported areas, and buyers are asked for a $1,000 non-refundable deposit for a December delivery window that is not guaranteed.

segments.title: Limits and unresolved questions
segments.body: The vehicle has no steering wheel or pedals, and Tesla says it will operate only in geofenced service areas. The order terms do not allow owners to use it commercially or put it on Tesla’s robotaxi network. Tesla has not explained how personal insurers would cover a vehicle without a human driver; a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration audit into its roadworthiness is pending.

perspectives.body: The Verge’s review of the offer highlights that cancelling the subscription would leave the Cybercab unusable on public roads, and that the federal safety audit is unresolved while deposits are being taken.

segments.title: Tesla’s price caveat
segments.body: TechCrunch reports that Elon Musk called the monthly fee “too high” and suggested it should be closer to $115. He also said nationwide availability would depend on regulatory approval; that broader rollout has not been established.

content.headline: Fake CAPTCHA prompts can trick users into installing malware
content.shortHeadline: Fake CAPTCHA prompts can install malware
content.standfirst: A scam called ClickFix imitates familiar website security checks, then asks users to run a sequence of keyboard commands that can infect their computer. The key warning: do not paste or run commands just to prove you are human.

image.caption: A fake verification prompt can use keyboard instructions to expose a computer to malware.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Prove you are not a robot’: how the Captcha scam captures your computer

segments.body: ClickFix scams imitate a website’s human-verification prompt but instruct visitors to press keys such as Windows+R, paste text and hit Enter. According to cybersecurity researcher Chris Fistonich, the sequence can run malicious code that the scam has copied to the computer’s clipboard.

segments.title: Pause before following prompts
segments.body: Unlike an ordinary image or text CAPTCHA, the fake check asks the user to carry out commands on their own device. The report advises pausing before following unfamiliar instructions, checking that security software is in place and contacting a bank promptly if a device has been compromised; changing passwords is also advised.

content.headline: FAA says routine equipment upgrade triggered US flight ground stop
content.shortHeadline: FAA traces US flight halt to equipment upgrade
content.standfirst: Officials say a router overloaded a critical communications system after a contractor replaced copper wire with fibre. The ground stop was lifted, but the FAA is still investigating the precise cause as cancellations continued.

sources.originalTitle: Transportation secretary blames ‘routine’ equipment upgrade for grounding flights nationwide

segments.body: The US flight ground stop followed a communications-system failure after a contractor upgraded a remote connection from copper wire to fibre-optic cable, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. A router then overloaded the system, according to officials; the FAA is conducting a root-cause analysis and has not determined whether the problem involved installation error or a faulty router.

segments.title: Disruption continued after flights resumed
segments.body: The ground stop was lifted, but Cirium reported more than 8,200 cancellations on Friday evening and at least 3,000 more on Saturday. Officials said the failure was an equipment issue and reported no evidence it was connected to AI, despite the timing of a separate FAA AI-tool announcement.

content.headline: Nvidia scandal raises questions about AI-chip exports and company oversight
content.shortHeadline: Nvidia scandal puts AI-chip exports under scrutiny
content.standfirst: Jensen Huang’s departure has intensified scrutiny of Nvidia’s links to Megaspeed, a company investigated over suspected chip diversion. New analysis says Chinese models show signs of training on restricted chips, but does not prove where they were used or that export rules were broken.

image.caption: Jensen Huang and Howard Lutnick shake hands at a G20 innovation ministerial in North Carolina.

sources.originalTitle: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models — uh-oh, Jensen!
Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
Pressure grows on Trump's Commerce Secretary Lutnick in fallout from Nvidia scandal
‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
Nvidia scandal: US treasury chief blames Lutnick’s commerce department over alleged lack of action
Where was Nvidia’s security team?

segments.body: Nvidia is facing questions about its oversight and the route by which advanced chips may have reached Chinese AI developers. The claims centre on Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-centre company investigated by US and Singapore authorities over suspected diversion. Megaspeed says it conducts lawful business; China has denied that Alice Huang, its former executive, was a spy.

segments.title: What the model analysis shows
segments.body: Will DePue of Unemployment Labs analysed the weights of openly released Chinese models and said he found signs that some had been trained on Nvidia Blackwell GPUs, which are restricted from export to China. That does not establish that the models were trained entirely on those chips or that export rules were violated: the hardware may have been used in offshore data centres.

perspectives.body: Georgetown researcher Sam Bresnick argues that controls focused on chip ownership or location may miss the possibility of Chinese firms accessing computing power through data centres in other countries.

segments.title: Oversight and wider consequences
segments.body: The allegations have prompted calls for congressional scrutiny of chip-export decisions and the Commerce Department’s handling of Megaspeed. Nvidia has hired a law firm to investigate, and federal inquiries are under way. In a separate analysis, a former Nvidia security chief’s departure prompted questions about what the company’s security team knew; the reporting does not establish that his departure was related.

perspectives.body: Retired intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades says corporate security teams can be poorly equipped to spot risks built through personal relationships and everyday contact. He says what Nvidia’s team knew, and whether it could have acted, remains unknown pending investigations.

content.headline: AI cameras flag nearly 19,000 possible driving offences in two-week trial
content.shortHeadline: AI cameras flag 19,000 possible driving offences
content.standfirst: A West Midlands trial detected possible seatbelt and mobile-phone offences, alongside other risky behaviour. No enforcement was planned from the trial, and police would still need to make decisions about any future action.

image.caption: A trial image shows a passenger holding an unrestrained child in the front seat.

sources.originalTitle: Wine-drinking driver among shocking images caught in AI camera trial

segments.body: AI-powered cameras used outside fire stations in Birmingham and Wolverhampton flagged nearly 19,000 potential driving offences in a two-week trial. The reported detections included more than 17,000 possible seatbelt offences and 1,920 possible mobile-phone offences; the system also recorded other behaviour, including a driver appearing to drink from a bottle of wine.

segments.title: Trial findings are not enforcement decisions
segments.body: The trial ended early because of the volume of detections, but no enforcement was planned from it. West Midlands officials are discussing whether the technology could be used more widely. A transport-safety researcher said such cameras could help identify where interventions are needed, while stressing that AI is not perfect and should support—not replace—police judgement.

content.headline: Protesters oppose 150MW data centre planned near Norfolk nature reserve
content.shortHeadline: Protesters challenge Norfolk data-centre plan
content.standfirst: The proposed Norwich-area facility would draw 150MW of power and be near wildlife areas. The developer says its design includes ecological protections and new planting; protesters dispute whether those measures will prevent harm.

image.caption: Protesters oppose plans for a large data centre outside Norwich.

sources.originalTitle: Protest over plan for data centre near nature site

segments.body: Hundreds of people protested against plans for a 150MW data centre at Keswick, outside Norwich, near Marston Marshes and other wildlife areas. The proposal says the facility would be powered by offshore wind. Protesters raised concerns about the effects of construction, noise and the site’s impact on local wildlife.

segments.title: Developer and residents differ
segments.body: Norwich Apex chief executive Matt Bartram says the plans include more than 15,000 trees, new hedgerows, habitat measures and acoustic screening informed by independent assessments. Protesters argue young trees cannot quickly replace mature ones and question whether noise and habitat impacts can be contained. Planning documents specify 72 rooftop chiller units.

perspectives.body: The developer says noise at nearby sensitive locations would remain at existing background levels and describes the scheme as an opportunity for jobs and digital infrastructure; those claims are contested by local opponents.

segments.title: Planning remains ahead
segments.body: Construction could begin next year if the proposal proceeds. The BBC reports that the developer says it takes local concerns about wildlife, trees and noise seriously; the supplied report does not say that planning approval has been granted.

content.headline: England face Spain test of progress after World Cup lessons
content.shortHeadline: England's progress faces its toughest test against Spain
content.standfirst: Thomas Tuchel says England are ready to test themselves against the world champions in Madrid. The Nations League meeting will show whether the team has moved on from its World Cup semi-final defeat.

image.caption: England head coach Thomas Tuchel during the World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina in Atlanta.

sources.originalTitle: Spain test will reveal if Tuchel and England have learned World Cup lessons
'No racism in Spain' – De la Fuente message for Tuchel

segments.body: England arrive in Madrid after four straight wins, including a 2-1 victory over Croatia, but Spain offer a far sterner measure. They are unbeaten in 43 matches and have won 34 of them; their last defeat was in March 2024.

segments.title: The match and its wider context
segments.body: Sunday's Nations League match will decide who finishes top of the group. England lost 3-2 to Spain at Wembley in September, and the visit also brings attention to racism in football: Tuchel said he did not expect incidents and would remind players of Uefa's protocol, while Spain coach Luis de la Fuente insisted there is no racism in Spain. The Spanish federation was fined last month after discriminatory chants at a match against Egypt.

content.headline: Wales end 73-year wait with historic 35-28 win over New Zealand
content.shortHeadline: Wales stun New Zealand to end a 73-year wait
content.standfirst: Wales beat New Zealand for the first time since 1953, ending a 34-match losing run against the All Blacks. A five-try performance and a remarkable defensive effort brought an emotional Cardiff celebration.

image.caption: New Zealand captain Beauden Barrett, who won his 149th cap against Wales.

sources.originalTitle: 'One of the greatest wins' - Wales stun All Blacks to go from no-hopers to heroes
All Blacks ran into a Welsh brick wall - Barrett

segments.body: Wales won 35-28 at the Principality Stadium, ending a 73-year wait for victory over New Zealand. They scored five tries and made 346 tackles, with Dafydd Jenkins making 38 as Wales held the All Blacks up over the line three times in the second half.

segments.title: New Zealand's response
segments.body: New Zealand coach Dave Rennie said his side had been out-passioned and were not clinical enough, adding that he expected a response at Twickenham. A bonus-point win there would secure the All Blacks top spot in the southern hemisphere table before South Africa play Ireland.

perspectives.body: Captain Beauden Barrett said Wales felt like a “brick wall” and praised the home crowd's influence, calling it one of the best places to play rugby.

content.headline: Will Joseph scores five tries as England thrash Japan 78-15
content.shortHeadline: Joseph's five-try return powers England past Japan
content.standfirst: Will Joseph marked his return to the England side with five tries in a 78-15 win over Japan. The result makes it four victories in a row as England prepare to face New Zealand.

image.caption: Will Joseph scores five tries as England beat Japan.

sources.originalTitle: Comeback kid Joseph thrills as England eye All Blacks

segments.body: England scored 13 tries in a 78-15 victory at Twickenham, with Will Joseph crossing five times. The 24-year-old had not played a Test since winning his first cap in 2022; he said it had been a challenging four years and that he was glad his work to return had paid off.

segments.title: A stronger test next
segments.body: It was England's fourth consecutive win after a run of five defeats, but New Zealand are next at Twickenham. England are also waiting on news about Ollie Chessum, Seb Atkinson and George Furbank, who are hoping to return from injury.

content.headline: Svitolina and Andreeva set up WTA Finals title match
content.shortHeadline: Svitolina and Andreeva reach the WTA Finals final
content.standfirst: Elina Svitolina swept past Linda Noskova to reach the final, where she will meet 19-year-old Mirra Andreeva. Aryna Sabalenka later apologised for an angry reaction during her defeat by Svitolina.

image.caption: Elina Svitolina, a three-time finalist at the WTA Finals.

sources.originalTitle: Svitolina races into WTA Finals showpiece against Andreeva
Sabalenka apologises & says viral comment 'not directed at Svitolina'

segments.body: Svitolina beat Wimbledon champion Noskova 6-2 6-1 in 64 minutes to reach her third WTA Finals final.
